newsitem.title: BURKINA FASO: Chirac, Nigeria's Abacha at Franco-African summit.
newsitem.headline: Chirac, Nigeria's Abacha at Franco-African summit.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac joined African leaders on Wednesday for the Franco-African summit meant to focus on good governance in Africa but overshadowed by conflict on the continent.
A surprising presence at the summit was Nigeria's military ruler General Sani Abacha, whose government is shunned by the West over human rights and democracy.
Burkina Faso television showed Abacha arriving and conference officials said it was the first time Nigeria had attended a Franco-African meeting at that level.

Chirac arrived in the dusty capital Ouagadougou 75 minutes behind schedule after chairing a security meeting at home following a bombing in a Paris subway that killed two people and injured scores on Tuesday night.
He went into talks shortly after his arrival with presidents of about 20 former French colonies. Talks involving a total of about 30 states open on Thursday.

Foreign ministers of the smaller group of states closest to Paris met earlier on Wednesday to fine-tune the summit agenda. The summits are held every two years, rotated between a French and African venue.
The ministers laboured for more than six hours on Tuesday night in the Burkina Faso capital to prepare resolutions on the main theme: good governance and development.

Burkina Faso Foreign Minister Ablasse Ouedreago said fighting in the Great Lakes region of Central Africa was discussed. There were frank exchanges between representatives of Burundi and of neighbouring states over the embargo imposed on Bujumbura following last July's coup.
He said the Ouagadougou meeting provided a good opportunity for Africans to discuss the succession to U.N. Secretary General Boutros Boutros-Ghali in order to keep the job on the continent.
But turmoil in Central Africa looked certain to dominate, and ministers pointed in this direction by adopting a text reaffirming the inviolability of Africa's colonial borders, delegates said.
A notable absentee will be Zaire's President Mobutu sese Seko, Africa's longest serving head of state, in power for 31 years. Mobutu is in France recuperating from cancer surgery.
Turmoil in his vast Central African nation and its charges that neighbours are backing rebels who have seized a swathe of territory, look certain to be hotly debated at the meeting.
Rwanda and Uganda are involved in the conflict in Zaire and fighting is raging in Burundi between the army and Hutu rebels.

Further north, the Central African Republic is mired in its third army mutiny this year. Its President Ange-Felix Patasse stayed away because of the two-week-old mutiny by soldiers in the capital demanding his resignation.
Patasse's spokesman Prosper Douba said Patasse expected "heads of state of friendly countries to send delegations and commissions of inquiry" to Bangui to assess the situation.

"We are expecting the summit to examine the situation and the heads of state to make a decision on it and condemn what is going on, because we know that the rebels benefit from the support of a number of friendly forces who supply them with arms and ammunition," Douba said.
In several French-speaking states, military coups or revolts have undermined the democratic gains of the early 1990s.
